# Rasters with `terra` {#sec-m2-raster}

A raster is a georeferenced matrix: elevation, slope, land use, satellite imagery,
population grid. The reference package is `terra`, the successor of `raster`.

```{r}
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

## Getting a digital elevation model

Instead of typing the coordinates of a rectangle by hand, we delimit the area from a
**real municipality**, with `geobr`, and let `elevatr` download the DEM for that area. We use
**Morretes (PR)**, because of the elevation change between the coast and the Serra do Mar (it is the same area
as the module's case study and the slope analysis in module 4), but the code
works for any municipality: just change `municipio_dem`/`uf_dem`.

```{r}
municipio_dem <- "Morretes"
uf_dem        <- "PR"

arquivo_dem <- "dados/brutos/dem_morretes.tif"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_dem)) {
  area_muni <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = uf_dem, year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE) |>
    dplyr::filter(name_muni == municipio_dem)

  # a 5 km margin around the municipality, so that the DEM has context
  # and does not stop exactly at the administrative boundary
  area <- area_muni |> sf::st_buffer(dist = 5000) |> sf::st_transform(4326)

  dem_raw <- elevatr::get_elev_raster(locations = area, z = 10, clip = "bbox")
  terra::writeRaster(terra::rast(dem_raw), arquivo_dem, overwrite = TRUE)
}

dem <- terra::rast(arquivo_dem)
dem
```

The object's printout already answers the essential questions: dimensions in cells, resolution,
extent, CRS and layer name.

```{r}
c(
  colunas    = ncol(dem),
  linhas     = nrow(dem),
  celulas    = terra::ncell(dem),
  camadas    = terra::nlyr(dem)
)
terra::res(dem)              # cell size, in the CRS unit
terra::crs(dem, describe = TRUE)$name
terra::global(dem, c("min", "max", "mean"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## DEM sources for official use

`elevatr` uses terrain *tiles* from AWS, derived from SRTM/Copernicus. They are great for
exploratory analysis and teaching, with no registration. For an official document, prefer a source
you can cite:

- **TOPODATA/INPE**: <https://data.inpe.br/dados/topodata/>. SRTM refined to 30 m, sheets
  by grid square, no registration. It is the most used reference in Brazilian studies.
- **Copernicus DEM GLO-30**: 30 m, global coverage, via OpenTopography.
- The procedure in the chapter is identical: `rast("caminho/do/arquivo.tif")`.
:::

## Visualising

```{r}
#| label: fig-dem-base
#| fig-cap: "Elevation of the Serra do Mar (m)"
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(dem, main = "Elevation (m)")
```

To integrate with `ggplot2` and combine with vector layers, use `tidyterra`:

```{r}
#| label: fig-dem-ggplot
#| fig-cap: "The same raster with tidyterra, over the municipal boundaries"
#| fig-height: 4.8
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_pr_sc.gpkg"
if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  muni <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "PR", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE),
    geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "SC", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE)
  )
  sf::st_write(muni, arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}
muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)

# view limits from the raster's own extent, not typed by hand:
# that way the map adjusts itself if you change municipio_dem to another place
zoom_dem <- sf::st_bbox(dem)

ggplot() +
  tidyterra::geom_spatraster(data = dem) +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom_dem[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = zoom_dem[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "turbo", na.value = NA, name = "Elevation (m)") +
  theme_void(base_size = 10)
```

## Crop and mask

These are two different operations, almost always used together:

- `crop()` reduces the **extent** to the geometry's rectangle;
- `mask()` turns everything **outside** the geometry into `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crop-mask
#| fig-cap: "crop (left) and crop + mask (right) by the municipality of Morretes"
#| fig-height: 3.6
morretes <- muni |> dplyr::filter(name_muni == "Morretes") |> sf::st_transform(terra::crs(dem))

dem_crop <- terra::crop(dem, terra::vect(morretes))
dem_mask <- terra::mask(dem_crop, terra::vect(morretes))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 4))
plot(dem_crop, main = "crop")
plot(dem_mask, main = "crop + mask")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

To check the crop over a real basemap (satellite, streets), `mapview` also accepts
rasters directly:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(dem_mask) + mapview::mapview(morretes, alpha.regions = 0)
```

`vect()` converts an `sf` object into `terra`'s vector format (`SpatVector`). It is the bridge
between the two packages; the other way round, `st_as_sf()`.

## Reproject, resample, aggregate

```{r}
terra::res(dem)         # before: in degrees, because the CRS is geographic (WGS 84)

# reproject: note the method - "bilinear" for continuous, "near" for categorical
dem_utm <- terra::project(dem, "EPSG:31982", method = "bilinear")
terra::res(dem_utm)     # after: in metres, in UTM 22S
```

The same cell size, about 0.00065°, becomes about 70 m after reprojection. That is
why measuring area, distance or slope requires a projected CRS: in degrees, "one cell"
has no fixed size on the ground.

```{r}
# aggregate: reduces the resolution (useful to speed up exploratory analyses)
dem_500 <- aggregate(dem_utm, fact = 5, fun = "mean")
c(original_m = terra::res(dem_utm)[1], agregado_m = terra::res(dem_500)[1])
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
terra::resample(a, b, method = "bilinear")   # puts `a` on the grid of `b` (essential for algebra)
terra::disagg(x, fact = 2)                   # increases the resolution (interpolates)
```

::: {.callout-important}
To compute between two rasters, they must be on the **same grid**: same CRS, same
resolution, same origin. That is what `resample()` is for. Without it, `r1 - r2` fails with "extents
do not match".
:::

## Raster algebra

```{r}
# arithmetic and logical operations are vectorised, cell by cell
acima_800 <- dem_utm > 800
terra::freq(acima_800)
```

```{r}
# reclassify into elevation bands
faixas <- matrix(c(
  -Inf,  50, 1,    # coastal plain
    50, 300, 2,    # lower slope
   300, 800, 3,    # slope
   800, Inf, 4     # plateau
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

dem_classes <- terra::classify(dem_utm, faixas)
terra::freq(dem_classes) |> dplyr::mutate(pct = round(100 * count / sum(count), 1))
```

The table says how much of the area is in each band; the map shows **where**:

```{r}
#| label: fig-dem-classes
#| fig-cap: "The DEM reclassified into four elevation bands"
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(dem_classes, type = "classes",
     levels = c("Coastal plain", "Lower slope", "Slope", "Plateau"),
     col = c("#2c7fb8", "#7fcdbb", "#fdae61", "#a6611a"),
     main = "Elevation bands")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
terra::app(x, fun = mean)                 # applies a function per cell across layers
terra::ifel(dem > 800, 1, 0)              # raster if-else
terra::focal(dem, w = 3, fun = "mean")    # moving window (smoothing, edge detection)
```

## Slope and terrain

`terra` computes terrain derivatives in one function. **Reproject to metres first**. In
degrees, the slope comes out wrong.

```{r}
terreno <- terra::terrain(dem_utm, v = c("slope", "aspect"), unit = "degrees")
terreno
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-declividade
#| fig-cap: "Elevation (left) and slope (right) in the Serra do Mar"
#| fig-height: 3.6
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 4))
plot(dem_utm, main = "Elevation (m)")
plot(terreno$slope, main = "Slope (degrees)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Side by side, it is clear that slope is not elevation: the plateau, which is high, is almost flat; what
stands out on the right is the mountain range's **escarpment**, the transition strip between the coast and
the plateau.

```{r}
terra::global(terreno$slope, c("mean", "max"), na.rm = TRUE) |> round(1)
```

In module 4 this raster is combined with road alignments to compare design alternatives.

## Extracting values by geometry

This is the operation that connects raster and vector. It is probably the most useful in the chapter.

```{r}
# by point: the elevation of each municipal seat, from geobr
# (instead of typing longitude/latitude by hand)
arquivo_sedes <- "dados/brutos/sedes_2022.gpkg"
if (!file.exists(arquivo_sedes)) {
  sf::st_write(geobr::read_municipal_seat(year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE),
               arquivo_sedes, quiet = TRUE)
}

sedes <- sf::st_read(arquivo_sedes, quiet = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::filter(name_muni %in% c("Curitiba", "Morretes", "Paranaguá")) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(dem_utm))

terra::vect(sedes)      # the same object, in terra's vector format

# what extract returns: a data.frame with one row per point, in the same order
alt_sedes <- terra::extract(dem_utm, terra::vect(sedes), ID = FALSE)
alt_sedes
```

The result does not include the municipality name: only the elevation, in the order of the points. That is why the
next step puts the name back with `bind_cols`:

```{r}
alt_sedes |>
  dplyr::bind_cols(local = sedes$name_muni) |>
  dplyr::rename(altitude_m = 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(altitude_m = round(altitude_m)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
# by polygon: zonal statistics, mean and maximum elevation by municipality
muni_serra <- muni |>
  dplyr::filter(name_muni %in% c("Morretes", "Antonina", "Paranaguá", "Piraquara", "Curitiba")) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(dem_utm))

zonal_alt <- terra::extract(dem_utm, terra::vect(muni_serra),
                     fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
zonal_alt     # one row per municipality, in the order of muni_serra
```

Again, only the value. The final table attaches the municipality name by position:

```{r}
muni_serra |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::transmute(municipio = name_muni,
            altitude_media_m = round(zonal_alt[[1]])) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(altitude_media_m)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
terra::extract(r, v, fun = "max")                  # another statistic
terra::extract(r, v, fun = mean, weights = TRUE)   # weights by the fraction of the cell in the geometry
terra::extract(r, v, exact = TRUE)                 # exact fraction (slower, more precise)
terra::zonal(r, terra::rasterize(v, r, "id"), fun = "mean")  # much faster on large datasets
```

## Writing and converting formats

```{r}
#| eval: false
terra::writeRaster(dem_utm, "resultados/dem_utm.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

# compressed GeoTIFF, which is what you deliver
terra::writeRaster(terreno$slope, "resultados/declividade.tif",
            overwrite = TRUE,
            gdal = c("COMPRESS=DEFLATE", "TILED=YES"))

# raster -> vector (class polygons; contours are in the next block)
poligonos <- terra::as.polygons(dem_classes) |> sf::st_as_sf()

# vector -> raster
grade <- terra::rasterize(terra::vect(muni_serra), dem_utm, field = "code_muni")

# raster -> table (for analysis in dplyr)
tabela <- as.data.frame(dem_utm, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Contour lines are the typical case of raster → vector conversion. Before delivering the
file, check on the map whether they follow the relief of the satellite image: switch the
basemap in the selector in the top-left corner and click on a contour to see the elevation.

```{r}
contornos <- terra::as.contour(dem_utm, levels = seq(0, 1600, by = 200))
contornos <- sf::st_as_sf(contornos)

mapview::mapview(contornos, zcol = "level", layer.name = "Elevation (m)",
                 map.types = c("Esri.WorldImagery", "OpenStreetMap"))
```

The conversion to a table deserves a mention: with `as.data.frame(r, xy = TRUE)` the raster becomes a
`data.frame` with columns `x`, `y` and the value. From there everything from module 1 applies. It is the
simplest way to answer questions such as "what is the elevation distribution in the right-of-way",
with `summarise` and `ggplot2`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Mind the size

A 30 m raster covering a state has hundreds of millions of cells. `as.data.frame()`
tries to bring all of it into memory. Crop (`crop`/`mask`) or aggregate (`aggregate`) first, and
prefer `extract`/`zonal`, which work without materialising the whole matrix.
:::
